methodological_rigor.justification: The qualitative exploratory design fits the aim of understanding sexuality and body image experiences after ovarian cancer treatment, and the manuscript describes semi-structured interviews, verbatim transcription, Kuckartz content analysis, reflexive protocols, and supervisor involvement. The main limitations are the very small sample of 12 German-speaking women, recruitment from patients already willing to complete sexuality items, and single-center context, all of which the authors acknowledge as limiting generalizability and representation. Statistical treatment is limited to descriptive participant characteristics and a reported median timing preference, which is acceptable for qualitative work but offers little quantitative inference or formal assessment of sampling uncertainty.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a small qualitative interview study without an intervention or comparative clinical outcome, so it fits Oxford level 4 as a descriptive case series-style clinical study. The topic is clinically relevant because all participants had ovarian cancer treated with surgery and chemotherapy, and the findings identify unmet needs in sexual health communication, partner support, stoma-related body image, and timing of clinician dialogue. Its translational value is plausible for survivorship care and guideline implementation, but it does not test whether any intervention improves quality of life or recovery.

reporting_quality.justification: A qualitative reporting framework rather than one of the schema-enumerated oncology standards is most applicable, so 'other' is appropriate. The manuscript reports recruitment source, eligibility criteria, interview duration and mode, transcription, MAXQDA analysis, coding approach, reflexive protocols, ethics approval, participant characteristics, and illustrative quotes, but it does not provide a formal qualitative checklist, full interview guide, or detailed audit trail. No public dataset or code is described; because interview transcripts are sensitive, reproducibility rests mainly on methods detail and quoted excerpts.

novelty_literature.justification: The novelty is a meaningful qualitative extension focused on ovarian cancer patients' lived experiences of sexuality, body image, and preferred timing of clinical conversations. The authors position the work against prior quantitative and qualitative studies on ovarian cancer sexual function, unmet needs, and psychosexual support, which limits claims of field-level novelty. Its main contribution is patient-centered granularity in a specific perioperative and survivorship context rather than a new mechanism or practice-changing intervention.

writing_presentation.justification: The abstract is clear and self-contained, and the results are organized around sexuality, body image, and support with somatic, psychological, and social subthemes. The manuscript uses participant quotations effectively, but some phrasing is awkward or repetitive, including duplicated wording in the limitations and occasional grammatical errors. Table captions are minimal in the normalized text, so the quoted material is useful but not fully standalone as presented.

key_strengths: Clinically important survivorship topic that is often under-addressed in ovarian cancer care.
Qualitative methods include verbatim transcription, inductive-deductive coding, reflexive protocols, and supervisor input.
Participant quotations support concrete themes around somatic changes, fertility, partner concerns, stoma-related body image, and timing of clinician dialogue.
key_concerns: Only 12 participants from a German-speaking, single-center, preselected group already willing to answer sexuality questions.
Findings are not linked to tested interventions or patient outcomes, limiting direct clinical actionability.
Reporting would benefit from a fuller qualitative checklist, complete interview guide, and clearer audit trail.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a useful and humane qualitative survivorship study with appropriate methods for an exploratory question, but the small selected sample and limited reproducibility detail keep it from a higher tier. At tier 3 it would need major revisions focused on qualitative reporting transparency and tighter claims.
